cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series
cards.body: Program 8 — Compassionate Mental Health Care

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: International mental health practice expects nurses to combine therapeutic engagement with structured assessment, evidence-based intervention, legal awareness, cultural safety and multidisciplinary collaboration.

bullets.label: This level bridges national nursing preparation
bullets.text: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations — strengthening your ability to manage complex presentations, apply local mental health law and support people across inpatient, community and general healthcare settings.

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: 9 CORE COMPETENCIES

bullets.label: Conduct mental state and risk assessments.
Formulate and communicate priority nursing concerns.
Manage suicide, self-harm, aggression and acute disturbance.
Recognise toxicity and serious adverse reactions.
Support physical health and substance-use conditions.
Apply least restrictive and lawful care principles.
Provide care with interpreters and family involvement.

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: By completing Level 2, you should be able to deliver safe, culturally responsive and evidence-informed mental health nursing while meeting the professional and legal expectations of international healthcare environments.

bullets.label: Risk assessment, crisis response and medication safety.
Legal compliance and professional confidence abroad.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation & Care Planning

bullets.label: Integrating mental state, history, physical
bullets.text: Integrating mental state, history, physical health, trauma, culture and risk to create individualised, person-centred nursing plans.

cards.title: What Does Comprehensive Assessment Include?
cards.body: International practice requires nurses to assess the whole person, not just presenting symptoms.

bullets.label: Assessment informs a shared formulation and individualised plan — not a diagnosis alone.

cards.title: Risk Formulation & Care Planning
cards.body: Risk Formulation

bullets.label: Consider current thoughts, behaviour, history,
bullets.text: Consider current thoughts, behaviour, history, dynamic triggers, protective factors and foreseeable changes. A numerical score should never replace clinical judgement.

bullets.label: Plans should identify goals, interventions,
bullets.text: Plans should identify goals, interventions, responsibilities and review timeframes. Include the person's preferences and make crisis plans practical and accessible.

bullets.label: Communicate current mental state, risk,
bullets.text: Communicate current mental state, risk, triggers, effective strategies, legal status, medication concerns and required follow-up clearly and completely.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: A woman with bipolar disorder presents with reduced sleep, rapid speech, impulsive spending and escalating conflict.

bullets.label: The nurse assesses physical health, substance
bullets.text: The nurse assesses physical health, substance use, risk, supports and previous relapse signs, then develops a shared plan with the multidisciplinary team.

bullets.label: Formulate risk — do not rely on a score alone

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm & Acute Behavioural Disturbance

bullets.label: Responding with calm, structure and legal awareness — preserving dignity, therapeutic engagement and future recovery.

cards.title: Suicide & Self-Harm Assessment
cards.body: Suicide Assessment

bullets.label: Assess ideation, plan, intent, access to means,
bullets.text: Assess ideation, plan, intent, access to means, past attempts, recent losses, intoxication, command hallucinations and protective factors. Collaborate on safety planning wherever possible.

bullets.label: Self-harm may serve functions such as relief
bullets.text: Self-harm may serve functions such as relief from overwhelming emotion. Address physical injury, immediate risk and underlying need — never punitive responses.

bullets.label: Escalating speech, pacing, threats,
bullets.text: Escalating speech, pacing, threats, intoxication and access to weapons require early intervention. Team communication and clear roles are essential.

cards.title: Assess risk
cards.body: Secure safety

bullets.label: Crisis response must be both timely and legally informed, with ongoing review of restrictive measures.
A patient states he has hidden tablets at home and plans to take them after discharge.
Nurse does not leave him alone
Involves supports with consent where possible
Take all stated plans and access to means seriously — engagement and safety must coexist.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health & Co-occurring Conditions

bullets.label: Monitoring the whole person — medications,
bullets.text: Monitoring the whole person — medications, physical illness and substance-related problems all influence mental state and risk.

cards.title: Psychotropic Medication Monitoring
cards.body: Antidepressants

bullets.label: Monitor for activation, worsening suicidality
bullets.text: Monitor for activation, worsening suicidality and serotonin toxicity. Educate patients on delayed onset of therapeutic effects.

bullets.label: Requires blood levels, renal and thyroid
bullets.text: Requires blood levels, renal and thyroid monitoring, stable fluid and salt intake. Know the signs of lithium toxicity — vomiting, tremor, confusion.

bullets.label: Monitor for movement disorders, metabolic
bullets.text: Monitor for movement disorders, metabolic effects, sedation and cardiac risk. Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness may indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

cards.title: Physical Health & Substance Use
cards.body: Physical Health Inequality

bullets.label: People with severe mental illness experience significant physical-health inequality. Nurses must actively monitor:
Weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
Alcohol, opioids, stimulants and other
bullets.text: Alcohol, opioids, stimulants and other substances cause intoxication, withdrawal and co-occurring mental illness. Severe withdrawal and overdose require urgent medical care.

bullets.label: Do not attribute all physical symptoms to mental illness — always investigate physical causes.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Legal, Ethical & Culturally Safe International Practice

bullets.label: Mental health law differs across jurisdictions
bullets.text: Mental health law differs across jurisdictions — but dignity, autonomy, confidentiality and least restrictive care remain universal principles.

cards.title: Core Legal & Ethical Principles
cards.body: Consent & Legal Status

bullets.label: Understand voluntary and involuntary care,
bullets.text: Understand voluntary and involuntary care, capacity, consent, review rights and documentation within the local jurisdiction.

bullets.label: Information is protected but may be shared when
bullets.text: Information is protected but may be shared when lawfully required to prevent serious harm. Always inform the person of its limits where possible.

bullets.label: Culture shapes explanations of distress,
bullets.text: Culture shapes explanations of distress, help-seeking and family roles. Ask respectfully — use professional interpreters for complex communication.

bullets.label: Involve families respectfully, always balancing
bullets.text: Involve families respectfully, always balancing consent, confidentiality and safety. Clear MDT roles improve continuity of care.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: An international nurse is unsure whether a patient can leave an inpatient unit.

bullets.label: Rather than relying on previous-country practice, the nurse:
Checks the person's current legal status
Seeks senior advice before taking action
Learn the law and policy of the jurisdiction
Always use the least restrictive lawful option
Explain confidentiality and its limits clearly
Ask rather than assume cultural preferences

cards.title: End-of-Programme Summary
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 8 — Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to:

bullets.label: Comprehensive mental state and risk assessment
Risk formulation and person-centred care planning
Crisis, medication safety and co-occurring conditions
Within international legal and cultural expectations
You are now prepared for Level 3 — where the focus moves to leadership, service improvement and global mental health.

cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8

cards.title: Section 1
cards.body: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning

bullets.label: International mental health practice expects
bullets.text: International mental health practice expects nurses to integrate mental state findings, history, physical health, trauma, substance use, culture and current risk. Assessment informs a shared formulation and an individualised care plan — not a diagnosis alone.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Gather mental, physical, social and cultural information systematically.
Build a nursing formulation that reflects the individual's unique context.
Balance and prioritise both mental and physical health priorities.
Convey assessment outcomes accurately to the multidisciplinary team.

cards.title: Comprehensive Assessment
cards.body: A thorough mental health assessment draws together multiple domains to build a complete clinical picture of the person.

bullets.label: Current symptoms, onset, duration and impact on daily functioning.
Appearance, mood, thought, perception, cognition and insight.
Comorbidities, medications, substance use and vital observations.
Trauma history, relationships, strengths, supports and cultural background.

cards.title: Risk Formulation
cards.body: Risk formulation is a clinical judgement process — not a numerical checklist. It considers the full picture of a person's situation to guide safe, proportionate care.

bullets.label: Active ideation, intent, plans and recent acts.
Past episodes, escalation patterns and known precipitants.
Supports, coping strengths and reasons for living.
Key principle: A numerical risk score must never replace clinical judgement. Formulate — don't just rate.

cards.title: Care Planning
cards.body: A good care plan is co-produced, actionable and regularly reviewed. It translates the formulation into clear goals and shared responsibilities.

bullets.label: Crisis and relapse-prevention plans must be
bullets.text: Crisis and relapse-prevention plans must be written in plain language — practical, accessible and meaningful to the person and their carers.

cards.title: Clinical Communication & Handover
cards.body: Effective handover keeps the whole team aligned on risk and recovery. Every handover should include:

bullets.label: Current presentation and any changes since last review.
Active risks, known triggers and effective de-escalation strategies.
Legal status, consent, medication concerns and PRN use.
Outstanding tasks, referrals and next scheduled review.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Bipolar Disorder — Manic Episode Presentation

bullets.label: A woman with bipolar disorder presents with
bullets.text: A woman with bipolar disorder presents with reduced sleep, rapid speech, impulsive spending and escalating interpersonal conflict — classic signs of a manic episode.

bullets.label: Physical health observations and vital signs
Social supports and previous relapse indicators
The nurse works collaboratively with the multidisciplinary team to:
Establish early warning signs with the person
Agree on sleep and activity targets
Coordinate medication review with the prescriber

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Formulate Risk — Don't Just Score It

bullets.label: Clinical judgement informed by context is always superior to a number alone.
Recovery-focused care highlights what the person brings, not only their difficulties.
Physical health must never be overlooked in mental health assessment.
Plans should be written with — and for — the person, in clear accessible language.

cards.title: GNPS · Programme 8 · Section 1
cards.body: Support Recovery.

bullets.label: You are now ready to apply comprehensive
bullets.text: You are now ready to apply comprehensive assessment, risk formulation and person-centred care planning in your mental health nursing practice.

cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 8 · Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

bullets.label: Section 2: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance

cards.title: Introduction
cards.body: High-risk mental health presentations require calm, structured and legally informed care. Nurses must respond to immediate risk while preserving:

bullets.label: Effective crisis care balances safety with compassion — never one at the expense of the other.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be equipped to:

bullets.label: Assess suicide and self-harm risk comprehensively and systematically
Respond to aggression and acute behavioural disturbance with structured interventions
Apply observation and environmental safety measures appropriately
Use the least restrictive interventions in all clinical scenarios

cards.title: Suicide Risk Assessment
cards.body: A thorough suicide assessment covers nine critical domains. No single factor determines risk — the full clinical picture guides the response.

bullets.label: Safety planning should be collaborative whenever possible — engage the patient as a partner in their own safety.

cards.title: Understanding Self-Harm
cards.body: Self-harm often serves a functional purpose — most commonly, relief from overwhelming emotional distress. Effective care addresses three layers:

bullets.label: Avoid punitive or dismissive responses — these undermine trust and increase long-term risk.
Assess and treat wounds promptly and without judgement
Evaluate ongoing danger and need for observation
Explore the emotional drivers and therapeutic supports

cards.title: Aggression & Violence Risk
cards.body: Early recognition of escalating behaviours is essential for safe de-escalation. Know the warning signs:

bullets.label: Raised voice, threatening language or rapid disorganised speech
Physical restlessness, clenched fists, invasion of personal space
Environmental risk factors that must be immediately mitigated
Clear roles and communication are essential in crisis response

cards.title: Observation & Restrictive Interventions
cards.body: Purposeful Observation

bullets.label: Monitor with a clear therapeutic rationale.
Record all actions and ongoing observations.
Debrief to evaluate and improve practice.
Every restrictive intervention must be justified, reviewed frequently and the least restrictive option available.
Observation is not passive — it should be therapeutic and goal-directed
Frequency and level of observation must be regularly reassessed
All decisions and actions require clear, contemporaneous records

cards.title: Clinical Example: Discharge Risk
cards.body: "A patient states he has hidden tablets at home and plans to take them after discharge."

bullets.label: Escalate to the treating team without delay
Develop a safety plan with the patient where possible
Record the stated plan, actions taken and supports involved

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Take Stated Plans Seriously

bullets.label: Access to means combined with a stated plan is a high-risk indicator — act immediately
Therapeutic alliance is a protective factor — preserve it while securing safety
Least restrictive practice demands ongoing reassessment, not a "set and forget" approach
Post-incident review supports staff wellbeing and continuous quality improvement

cards.title: Section Summary
cards.body: "Calm. Structured. Compassionate."

bullets.label: Safe mental health nursing in high-risk
bullets.text: Safe mental health nursing in high-risk presentations is built on clinical skill, legal literacy and therapeutic presence. Carry these principles into every interaction.

cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8

bullets.label: Section 3: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: Support Recovery. Promote Wellbeing.

bullets.label: People using mental health services may
bullets.text: People using mental health services may experience medication effects, physical illness, and substance-related problems that directly influence mental state and risk. International nurses are expected to monitor and support the whole person.

bullets.label: Addressing inequality in severe mental illness

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: After completing this section, you will be
bullets.text: After completing this section, you will be equipped to manage complex clinical scenarios with confidence and clinical rigour.

bullets.label: Apply safe monitoring protocols for common psychiatric medications
Identify serious toxicity and red-flag clinical presentations
Screen and respond to metabolic and cardiovascular risk
Recognise withdrawal states and co-occurring mental illness

cards.title: Antidepressants & Mood Stabilisers
cards.body: Monitoring is essential throughout treatment — especially early on when risk is highest.

bullets.label: Monitor for behavioural activation and agitation
Watch for worsening suicidality, particularly in the first 1–2 weeks
Recognise signs of serotonin toxicity: agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, clonus
Regular serum lithium levels (therapeutic range: 0.6–1.0 mmol/L)
Stable fluid and salt intake — dehydration raises toxicity risk
Educate patients on early toxicity signs

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Antipsychotics: What to Monitor

bullets.label: Parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia — assess using standardised tools (e.g. AIMS)
Weight gain, raised blood glucose, dyslipidaemia — especially with clozapine and olanzapine
QTc prolongation risk — baseline ECG required for some agents; monitor sedation levels
Fever, muscular rigidity, altered consciousness — a medical emergency. Stop antipsychotic immediately
NMS is rare but life-threatening. Any
bullets.text: NMS is rare but life-threatening. Any combination of fever, rigidity and altered consciousness in a patient on antipsychotics must trigger urgent escalation.

cards.title: Physical Health Monitoring
cards.body: Addressing the Health Inequality Gap

bullets.label: People with severe mental illness die on
bullets.text: People with severe mental illness die on average 15–20 years earlier than the general population — largely from preventable physical conditions.

cards.title: Physical Health
cards.body: Metabolic & Cardiovascular Risk Profile

bullets.label: Structured annual physical health checks are a nursing priority for all people on long-term psychotropic medication.

cards.title: Co-occurring Substance Use
cards.body: Substance use and mental illness frequently co-exist. Nurses must be able to recognise intoxication, withdrawal and dual-diagnosis presentations.

bullets.label: Withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium
bullets.text: Withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium tremens — a medical emergency requiring urgent intervention and CIWA monitoring

bullets.label: Overdose presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, unconsciousness — naloxone is first-line reversal
Cocaine and amphetamines can trigger psychosis, tachycardia and hyperthermia — monitor cardiac status closely

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Lithium Toxicity: A Case in Practice

bullets.label: A man taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse
bullets.text: A man taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor and confusion following a period of dehydration — classic signs of lithium toxicity.

bullets.label: Withhold further lithium doses as per policy
Request serum lithium level and renal function tests
Document clearly and escalate via SBAR
Withhold lithium, escalate to medical team immediately
Urgent bloods including serum lithium level
Never attribute confusion or tremor solely to
bullets.text: Never attribute confusion or tremor solely to psychiatric illness in a patient on lithium. Always consider toxicity first.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Take these clinical priorities into every practice setting.

bullets.label: Psychotropic toxicity can escalate rapidly — recognise early signs and act swiftly
Do Not Attribute All Symptoms to Mental Illness
Physical causes must always be considered and ruled out systematically
Annual checks save lives — address the physical health inequality gap proactively
Treat Severe Withdrawal as a Medical Emergency
Alcohol and opioid withdrawal can be fatal — escalate early and document clearly

cards.title: Compassionate Mental Health Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 8

bullets.label: Section 4: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice

cards.title: Our Guiding Purpose
cards.body: "Support recovery. Promote wellbeing."

bullets.label: Mental health law and policy differ across
bullets.text: Mental health law and policy differ across jurisdictions, but core principles remain universal. As an internationally qualified nurse, understanding the local legal framework is essential before independent practice begins.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Understand and apply local mental health legislation and professional standards within your jurisdiction.
Navigate the tension between autonomy, confidentiality, and patient safety with confidence and clarity.
Deliver care that is trauma-informed, culturally responsive, and person-centred at all times.
Work effectively with families and multidisciplinary teams to ensure continuity and quality of care.

cards.title: Consent and Legal Status
cards.body: What Nurses Must Understand

bullets.label: Nurses must be familiar with the distinction
bullets.text: Nurses must be familiar with the distinction between voluntary and involuntary care, and what each means for patient rights and nursing responsibilities.

bullets.label: Assess and document mental capacity accurately
Obtain valid, informed consent before care
Know the patient's right to review and appeal legal status
Never assume prior-country processes apply. Always verify legal status locally.

cards.title: Confidentiality and Its Limits
cards.body: Protected — but Not Absolute

bullets.label: Patient information is legally and ethically
bullets.text: Patient information is legally and ethically protected. However, disclosure may be lawfully required to prevent serious harm to the patient or others.

bullets.label: Share information only on a need-to-know basis
Inform the patient about confidentiality limits before they disclose, wherever possible
Document all decisions and rationale clearly
Follow your jurisdiction's specific reporting obligations

cards.title: Cultural Safety in Mental Health Nursing
cards.body: Culture profoundly shapes how individuals understand distress, seek help, and involve family. Culturally safe practice means asking — not assuming.

bullets.label: Explore the patient's own explanations of their distress without judgement or assumption.
For complex clinical communication, always use qualified interpreters — never family members as substitutes.
Acknowledge that family involvement varies culturally. Balance cultural norms with individual consent and safety.

cards.title: Family and Multidisciplinary Collaboration
cards.body: Working Together for Better Outcomes

bullets.label: Families often hold vital context about the
bullets.text: Families often hold vital context about the patient's history, triggers, and strengths. Involving them thoughtfully strengthens care planning and recovery.

bullets.label: Respect the patient's consent before sharing information with family
Clarify each team member's role to avoid duplication or gaps
Maintain consistent, documented communication across disciplines
Ensure handovers are clear and safety-focused

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Applying the Framework in Practice

bullets.label: An international nurse is unsure whether a
bullets.text: An international nurse is unsure whether a patient can leave an inpatient unit. Rather than defaulting to prior-country practice, the nurse checks the patient's legal status, reviews local policy, and seeks senior clinical advice before taking any action.

bullets.label: Confirm patient rights and detention authority.
Consult hospital and regional discharge rules.
Escalate to supervisor or legal counsel.
This approach protects both the patient's
bullets.text: This approach protects both the patient's rights and the nurse's professional accountability — regardless of prior international experience.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Know the Law

bullets.label: Learn the mental health legislation and
bullets.text: Learn the mental health legislation and professional standards specific to your jurisdiction before practising independently.

bullets.label: Always choose the least restrictive lawful approach that meets the patient's clinical and safety needs.
Be transparent with patients about what is
bullets.text: Be transparent with patients about what is protected and when disclosure may be required — before they share sensitive information.

bullets.label: Cultural preferences are individual. Ask
bullets.text: Cultural preferences are individual. Ask respectfully, listen carefully, and never impose assumptions based on background.

cards.title: GNPS Programme 8 · Section 4
cards.body: Ready to Practise with Confidence?

bullets.label: Legal, ethical, and culturally safe practice is
bullets.text: Legal, ethical, and culturally safe practice is not a checklist — it is a professional mindset. Carry these principles into every clinical encounter.

bullets.label: Complete the Section 4 reflective activities and case-based assessments in your GNPS learner workbook.
Review your local jurisdiction's mental health legislation, nursing council standards, and cultural safety frameworks.
Discuss complex cases with your clinical supervisor or senior nurse to build confidence in applying these principles.
